name: cweb
desc: Literate documentation system for C, C++, and Java
why: Knuth's literate programming system, weaving code and documentation into a single source file, is a genuinely odd and historic idea.

brief.what_it_is: CWEB is a literate programming system for documenting C, C++, and Java programs. You write one source file, foo.w, that mixes prose documentation with code. CTANGLE reads that file and produces a compilable program file, foo.c. CWEAVE reads the same file and produces foo.tex, a prettily printed, cross-indexed document for TeX. The homepage describes two programs, ctangle and cweave, and the brew package provides those two executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The authors frame it as treating a program as a communication to human beings rather than as a set of instructions to a computer. The homepage says WEB was developed by Donald E. Knuth while he wrote TeX, and that CWEB adapts it to C (Silvio Levy, 1987) and later to C++ and ANSI C.
brief.how_it_works: CTANGLE extracts the code from the .w file into a compilable .c file. CWEAVE typesets the documentation and code into a .tex file with cross-references and an index. Since version 3.61 the weaver can also produce PDF with clickable links, either through standard TeX with dvipdfm or through pdfTeX.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers the CWEB software by anonymous ftp from ftp.cs.stanford.edu, in the ~ftp/pub/cweb directory, as cweb.tar.gz. The page does not describe a build procedure, and it does not mention the brew package. For PDF output you need TeX plus either dvipdfm or pdfTeX. The page points to the Makefile for examples of the PDF workflow. The page also links the CWEB development project maintained by Andreas Scherer, which the authors say carries the current news and newer versions.
brief.standout: The source file is a hypertext document as much as a program, and the page presents the cross-indexed typeset output as a core deliverable. The authors also say CTANGLE and CWEAVE are now finished and will not change, which is an unusual stance for a developer tool.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage says CTANGLE and CWEAVE are stable and the authors do not intend to change CWEB unless a devastating bug is found. The most recent version it names is 3.64, with a 3.6 cover edition and a 2001 printing. The page carries no release dates. Ongoing development of CWEB 4.0 is referred to the separate CWEB development project, which I did not fetch.
brief.caveats: The homepage is an authors' page for the 1993 Knuth and Levy book, and its details may be dated. The book is out of print. The page warns that identifiers such as and, compl, not, or, xor, and not_eq became reserved in newer C++, so old .w files may format strangely; the fix is a line like @s not_eq normal. The authors describe some non-catastrophic infelicities as permanent features. I did not check the brew formula or how well the build works on other platforms.
quotes: The main idea is to regard a program as a communication to human beings rather than as a set of instructions to a computer.
The authors do not intend to change CWEB henceforth unless some devastating new bug is discovered.
If you are in the software industry and do not use CWEB but your competitors do, your competitors will soon overtake you---and you'll miss out on a lot of fun besides.
fetch_log: https://cs.stanford.edu/~knuth/cweb.html: fetched OK, the homepage text was read in full. No README or docs page was followed, and the CWEB development project link was not fetched.

judge.reason: CWEB makes one source file both a working C program and a cross-indexed human-readable document, offering a distinctive, hands-on introduction to literate programming.

entry.title: cweb
entry.tldr: Knuth and Levy's literate programming system: write one file of prose and C, then get both a compilable program and a typeset, cross-indexed document.
entry.deeper_look:
CWEB works from a single source file, `foo.w`, that mixes explanation with code. Two programs read it. `ctangle` pulls the code out and writes `foo.c`, ready for a compiler. `cweave` takes the same file and writes `foo.tex`, a typeset document with cross-references and an index. Since version 3.61 the weaver can also produce PDF with clickable links, through standard TeX with dvipdfm or through pdfTeX.

The idea comes from WEB, which Donald Knuth developed while writing TeX. Silvio Levy adapted it to C in 1987, and it later grew to cover C++ and ANSI C. The stated premise: "The main idea is to regard a program as a communication to human beings rather than as a set of instructions to a computer." You order the program for a reader, not for the compiler, and the tools rearrange it afterwards.

That inversion is the door. Once you write code in the order you would explain it, comments stop being an afterthought and the source becomes a document someone can read start to finish. Much of the later literate programming and notebook tradition descends from this approach.

The tools are old and declared finished. The authors say they do not intend to change CWEB "unless some devastating new bug is discovered." For a developer tool, that is a rare stance. Work on a CWEB 4.0 continues in a separate development project that the homepage links.
entry.install:
brew install cweb
# PDF output also needs TeX, plus dvipdfm or pdfTeX

try_this.what_happens: Shows how ctangle is invoked; it is the half that turns a .w file into compilable C.
Shows how cweave is invoked; it is the half that turns a .w file into a TeX document.

entry.whats_unique: One file is both the program and its cross-indexed typeset explanation, and the original authors consider the tools complete and frozen.
entry.caveats: The homepage is the authors' page for a 1993 book that is out of print, and old .w files may format oddly because newer C++ reserves words like `not` and `xor`; a line like `@s not_eq normal` fixes it.
